title: Doctors Urge Early Action on Malaria and Dengue as India's Monsoon Season Peaks
excerpt: Health experts warn that dismissing early symptoms as routine viral fever is the most common and dangerous mistake during monsoon months, when all Indian states except Ladakh are endemic to mosquito-borne diseases.
body:
• Doctors across India are urging early testing and treatment for malaria and dengue as monsoon season drives a surge in mosquito-borne infections
  • Malaria symptoms often mimic common viral fevers, leading to dangerous treatment delays; the disease follows a distinctive recurring fever pattern that distinguishes it from flu
  • Dengue warning signs requiring immediate medical attention include persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, mucosal bleeding, and a sudden drop in platelet count
  • India reduced malaria cases by 78% between 2015 and 2024, but all states except Ladakh remain endemic to both dengue and chikungunya during monsoon months

As India's monsoon season reaches its peak, doctors are raising alarms about the rising number of malaria and dengue cases and stressing that early recognition of warning signs can mean the difference between a routine recovery and a medical emergency.

Health experts say one of the most common — and most dangerous — mistakes during monsoon season is dismissing the first symptoms of mosquito-borne diseases as a routine viral fever, delaying the testing and treatment that could prevent severe complications.

The Viral Fever Trap

Malaria typically begins with a combination of fever, chills, headache, and fatigue that closely resembles influenza or a common cold. What distinguishes it, doctors say, is the pattern: unlike a steady viral fever, malaria produces a distinctive cycling rhythm in which fever rises, falls, and returns.

"Patients often present with what appears to be a mild illness, but malaria typically begins with a combination of fever, chills, headache, and profound fatigue, which can easily be mistaken for flu or dengue," said Dr. Suchismitha Rajamanya. "The key lies in how these symptoms behave over time."

Ignoring this pattern often leads to delays in testing, giving the malaria parasite more time to multiply in the bloodstream. Doctors recommend seeking testing if fever persists for more than two days, especially when accompanied by the recurring pattern of chills and sweating.

Dengue: The Dangerous Defervescence Phase

With dengue, the danger can actually increase as the fever begins to subside. The defervescence phase — when body temperature starts to drop — is precisely when severe dengue complications can emerge, including plasma leakage, hemorrhaging, and organ dysfunction.

Warning signs that require immediate hospitalization include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, mucosal bleeding (nosebleeds, gum bleeds, or bruising), a rapid drop in platelet count, lethargy or restlessness, and reduced urine output. For children, the Indian Academy of Pediatrics emphasizes cautious intravenous fluid therapy, as excessive fluids during the capillary leak phase can worsen respiratory distress.

There is currently no specific antiviral therapy for dengue. Management centers on adequate hydration, monitoring of hematocrit and platelet counts, fever management, and strict avoidance of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin, which can worsen bleeding.

India's Progress and Persistent Risk

India has made substantial strides against malaria, cutting cases by 78% and deaths by roughly the same proportion between 2015 and 2024. Between 2022 and 2024, 160 districts recorded zero malaria cases. The government's National Strategic Plan for Malaria Elimination targets eradication by 2030.

But the monsoon season remains dangerous. All states and Union territories except Ladakh are endemic to both dengue and chikungunya, with the highest risk of outbreaks during and immediately after the monsoon months. The Union health ministry has directed states to intensify preventive measures, including community awareness drives through municipal corporations and local bodies.

Prevention Basics for Monsoon Season

Public health authorities recommend removing or emptying all stagnant water sources weekly, using mosquito repellents and window screens, wearing full-sleeve clothing during dawn and dusk, and sleeping under mosquito nets. Hospitals have been directed to ensure adequate stocks of diagnostic kits, drugs, and dedicated isolation wards.

For NRIs planning monsoon-season visits to India, doctors advise consulting a travel health specialist before departure, carrying insect repellent containing DEET or picaridin, and seeking immediate medical testing if fever develops during or after the trip. Early diagnosis remains the single most effective defense against both diseases.
